title: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy with a peculiar CSF biomarker profile in an 89-year-old man
case_prompt:
An 89-year-old man, previously healthy and living independently, was evaluated for a 6-month history of difficulty walking on uneven ground and a 1-month history of intermittent episodes of disorientation and amnesia accompanied by moderate balance impairment. He had known obstructive asthma, bilateral hearing loss, cataracts, and eczema; he was a former smoker.

On initial evaluation, neurologic examination and noncontrast head CT were unremarkable. Mini–Mental State Examination (MMSE) was 30/30; clock drawing was normal. Consortium to Establish a Registry for Alzheimer’s Disease (CERAD) testing revealed only decreased verbal fluency (8 points) and delayed word recall (62%).

Two months later, he was admitted with severe balance and cognitive impairments and urinary and fecal incontinence. MMSE was 15/30; CERAD testing was abnormal in 8 of 10 categories. Brain MRI without gadolinium showed bilateral hippocampal atrophy (2/4) without other temporomedial atrophy. On examination, he was alert but disoriented to time and place, spoke in a low voice, had slight upward gaze restriction, static tremor of the upper extremities, a pronounced startle response with eyes closed, brisk tendon reflexes, and a slow, wide-based gait. No myoclonus was observed. EEG showed only slight generalized disturbance.

Laboratory evaluation revealed an elevated serum anti-thyroglobulin antibody titer with normal thyroid function tests and negative onconeuronal antibodies. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis demonstrated a slight lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and a positive protein 14-3-3 assay. Infectious studies and bacterial cultures of CSF were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease was considered because of the subacute dementia and positive CSF 14-3-3, but “Protein 14-3-3 has high sensitivity for detecting CJD. However, it has been reported to be positive in many other neurological disorders … disturbingly often even in patients with treatable conditions.”  
2. Alzheimer’s disease was considered given the memory impairment and later CERAD findings, but “now showing a typical profile of Alzheimer’s disease” occurred only after steroids and the time course was more rapid than typical AD.  
3. Infectious encephalitis was evaluated due to CSF pleocytosis, but “Bacterial staining and culturing Negative” and “Infectious agents Negative.”  
4. Paraneoplastic encephalitis was considered, but “Onconeuronal antibodies Negative.”  
5. Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT) was supported by positive anti-thyroglobulin antibodies and rapid improvement after a steroid trial, as “with positive TG antibodies and response to corticosteroids, our patient falls well within the limits of SREAT.”
